chapter_summary:
After a predictive design has been completed, or in an existing environment where performance issues are present, a **passive site survey** becomes invaluable. Unlike a predictive survey that models the environment, a passive survey actively listens to the existing RF landscape. It's like taking a snapshot of all Wi-Fi activity in a given area without actively communicating with any access points. This allows you to understand the real-world conditions, validate your predictive assumptions, and uncover issues that simulations might miss, such as unexpected interference or rogue devices.

The methodology for a passive survey involves systematically walking through the survey area with a specialized kit. Your **hardware setup** typically includes a laptop running site survey software (e.g., Ekahau AI Pro, NetSpot), equipped with one or more external Wi-Fi adapters. These adapters are crucial because they offer better sensitivity and consistency than internal laptop Wi-Fi cards, and some allow for simultaneous scanning of multiple channels across both 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands. The laptop needs to be configured to prevent its internal Wi-Fi from connecting to any networks, ensuring the external adapters are solely used for scanning. A key aspect of the physical walk-through is maintaining a consistent pace and orientation of the survey kit to capture accurate, repeatable data.

As you walk, the survey software, linked to your external Wi-Fi adapters, continuously **collects and interprets real-time RF data**. For each data point (often marked by clicking on the floor plan as you move), the software records:
*   **RSSI (Received Signal Strength Indicator):** This is the raw signal power from all detected access points. You'll see heatmaps showing the signal strength from your intended APs, as well as signals from neighboring networks. The goal is to ensure that your target RSSI (e.g., -67 dBm for voice, -70 dBm for data) is met across the entire coverage area. Areas with RSSI below your target indicate coverage gaps.
*   **SNR (Signal-to-Noise Ratio):** This is arguably more important than RSSI alone. SNR measures the ratio of the desired signal strength to the background noise level. A strong signal (good RSSI) can still result in poor performance if the noise floor is also high. For example, an RSSI of -60 dBm with a noise floor of -90 dBm yields an excellent SNR of 30 dB. However, an RSSI of -60 dBm with a noise floor of -70 dBm results in a poor SNR of 10 dB, which will lead to frequent retransmissions and slow speeds. You're looking for an SNR of at least 20-25 dB for general data and 25-30 dB or higher for high-bandwidth or latency-sensitive applications like VoIP.
*   **Noise Floor:** This represents the ambient background RF energy in the environment. A high noise floor (e.g., -80 dBm or higher) indicates significant RF interference, which could be from other Wi-Fi networks, non-Wi-Fi devices, or environmental factors. Identifying the noise floor helps in calculating SNR and understanding the overall RF cleanliness of the environment.
*   **Channel Utilization:** This metric shows how busy each Wi-Fi channel is. High channel utilization (e.g., consistently above 50-60%) indicates congestion, which can lead to performance bottlenecks even with good signal strength. Passive surveys help identify channels that are heavily used by neighboring networks or your own APs, informing better channel planning decisions.

One of the critical benefits of a passive survey is its ability to **detect and identify potential sources of Wi-Fi interference**.
*   **Co-channel Interference (CCI):** This occurs when multiple APs (either your own or from neighboring networks) operate on the same channel in overlapping coverage areas. The passive survey will show multiple APs on the same channel with strong RSSI in the same location. This leads to contention for airtime, reducing overall throughput.
*   **Adjacent Channel Interference (ACI):** This happens when APs operate on partially overlapping channels (e.g., channel 1 and channel 2 in 2.4 GHz). While less severe than CCI, ACI still degrades performance. Passive surveys visualize the channels in use, making ACI apparent.
*   **Rogue Access Points:** These are unauthorized APs connected to your network, often unknowingly by employees, or malicious APs set up by attackers. A passive survey will detect these APs broadcasting SSIDs that are not part of your authorized network. Identifying rogue APs is a critical security function, as they can create backdoors into your wired network or be used for man-in-the-middle attacks. The survey software can often pinpoint their physical location on the floor plan.

**Common mistakes** in passive surveys include rushing the walk-through, not taking enough data points, holding the survey kit inconsistently, or failing to use an external Wi-Fi adapter. Another mistake is relying solely on RSSI without considering SNR or noise floor, which can mask underlying performance issues. Safety notes: Ensure your laptop is fully charged or has a portable power bank. Be mindful of your surroundings while walking and looking at the screen, especially in busy or unfamiliar environments. Always secure your equipment to prevent drops or theft. The data collected during a passive survey forms the basis for refining your AP placement, adjusting transmit power, and optimizing channel assignments to deliver a high-performing, reliable, and secure WLAN.

screens.title: Conducting a Passive Site Survey
screens.subtitle: Listen first, decide second — measuring the real RF environment without joining networks

narration.text: A passive site survey is a focused listening exercise that captures how Wi‑Fi actually behaves in a space. Instead of connecting to access points, you record existing signals, noise, and channel use so you can validate predictive models and find problems simulation might miss. In practice this means walking a planned route with a survey laptop and external Wi‑Fi adapter(s) that only scan and log. You will learn to collect RSSI, SNR, noise floor, and channel utilization, and to interpret what those numbers imply for coverage and capacity. You’ll also learn to spot interference patterns like co‑channel and adjacent‑channel contention, and to identify rogue access points that present security risks. During this lesson we’ll also cover the necessary hardware and software setup, how to maintain a repeatable walk pace and orientation, and the top mistakes that reduce data quality. By the end you will be able to plan and execute a passive survey, review heatmap outputs, and use the survey data to make concrete placement, power, and channel adjustments. Think of this as taking an accurate photo of the wireless air — it tells where the network is healthy and where it needs work.

You will explain the survey methodology and why passive measurement is chosen when validating a predictive design or troubleshooting an existing environment. You will identify and configure the hardware and software components needed for consistent, repeatable scans, including the use of external adapters and preventing your laptop from associating with networks. You will collect and interpret key RF metrics — RSSI, SNR, noise floor, and channel utilization — and use them to diagnose coverage or capacity problems. screens.title: What a passive site survey is and isn't
screens.subtitle: Definition, purpose, and when to choose passive measurement

narration.text: A passive site survey is a method of collecting RF information by listening to existing Wi‑Fi transmissions without associating to any access point. It captures the real ambient activity on every channel the adapter can see, which makes it ideal after a predictive design or when troubleshooting a live environment. This means you gather evidence of what is actually happening in the air: who is transmitting, how strong the signals are, and how busy channels are. A passive survey is not a load test or an active throughput check; it does not generate traffic or measure end‑user throughput. Instead, it provides the factual inputs you need to diagnose coverage gaps, interference, and unauthorized devices. A common misconception is that a strong RSSI alone guarantees good performance. Passive surveys help avoid that trap by adding the noise floor and channel utilization context. For example, you might see -60 dBm RSSI but also a high noise floor producing poor SNR; that tells you the channel is noisy despite apparent signal strength. The practical outcome of a passive survey is a set of heatmaps and channel charts that guide changes to AP placement, transmit power, and channel assignments.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Passive surveys listen only; they reveal real transmission patterns, interference, and unauthorized APs without associating to the network.

content.html:
Core Concept
What passive surveying is

A passive survey records existing Wi‑Fi signals by listening. It produces heatmaps and channel charts that represent real, on‑the‑air activity to validate predictions and find problems predictions miss.

Key trait: No association — scanning only
Common output: RSSI, SNR, noise floor, channel utilization maps
Misconception: Strong RSSI alone equals good performance
Analogy & example
Think of a passive survey as taking a photograph of the air. The image shows who else is in the room and how noisy it is. For instance, a predictive model might assume no neighbor networks, but a passive snapshot can show nearby APs and high utilization you didn’t expect.
Concrete example
Validated predictive design
After running a passive survey you compare heatmaps to the predictive plan and mark areas where RSSI or SNR fall short, then adjust AP locations or power.
Key Takeaway

Passive data is ground truth for coverage, interference, and rogue device detection.

screens.title: The passive survey walk‑through methodology
screens.subtitle: Planning, walking, and capturing repeatable data

narration.text: A high‑quality passive survey depends on a disciplined walk methodology. Begin by loading a floor plan into your survey software and marking the planned route or grid you will follow. Ensure the laptop has external adapters attached and that internal Wi‑Fi is disabled to prevent accidental associations. Keep a consistent pace and orientation as you walk so that time‑stamped samples map accurately to location markers — inconsistent speed or orientation can produce noisy heatmaps that are hard to interpret. Many practitioners click to mark sample points as they move, or allow continuous sampling if the software supports it, but in all cases maintain steady movement and avoid stopping in one spot for long periods. Record metadata such as time, adapter used, and any unusual events like heavy human traffic or nearby machinery, because such context helps later analysis. Finally, repeat the walk if possible to verify repeatability. A repeated pass showing similar heatmap patterns increases confidence in your findings and prevents false positives caused by transient signals. The passive survey walk‑through methodology means plan the route, use external adapters, maintain steady pace and orientation, record context, and repeat the walk to ensure reliable, repeatable data.. In practical terms, planning, walking, and capturing repeatable data. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Methodology
keyIdea.text: Plan the route, use external adapters, maintain steady pace and orientation, record context, and repeat the walk to ensure reliable, repeatable data.

content.html:
Process Flow
Planning and walking
1. Load floor plan and mark route.
2. Attach external adapters; disable internal Wi‑Fi association.
3. Maintain consistent pace and device orientation while sampling.
4. Record metadata and repeat for verification.
Why repeatability matters

Consistent walking produces heatmaps that can be compared across time or after network changes. Inconsistent speed or orientation causes sample clustering or gaps that obscure real problems.

Example
Click vs continuous sampling
Clicking to mark points can help create precise locations on a floor plan, while continuous sampling is quicker but depends on steady motion to map correctly.
Key Takeaway

A repeatable walk is as important as the hardware — data without consistency is unreliable.

screens.title: Hardware and software essentials
screens.subtitle: Selecting adapters, configuring the laptop, and software choices

narration.text: The survey kit is the heart of the passive survey. A typical setup includes a laptop with site survey software and one or more external Wi‑Fi adapters. External adapters improve sensitivity and consistency compared to internal laptop cards, and some adapters allow wider channel coverage or better reception. Choose adapters known to work well with your chosen survey software, and confirm the software recognizes them. Configure the laptop so its internal Wi‑Fi is disabled or prevented from associating. If the laptop joins a network during the walk, the captured data will be corrupted by local traffic and state changes. Popular survey tools mentioned in the chapter include software that can display heatmaps and channel utilization. Before you start the walk, verify battery or external power, secure cables so you don’t trip, and confirm adapter placement yields consistent orientation. Small differences in adapter position or laptop orientation can change readings, so standardize how you carry the kit. A well‑prepared kit reduces measurement error and saves time when analyzing results. Hardware and software essentials means use external adapters with recognized software, disable internal wi‑fi associations, and standardize adapter placement and power to gather consistent data.. In practical terms, selecting adapters, configuring the laptop, and software choices. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Survey kit
keyIdea.text: Use external adapters with recognized software, disable internal Wi‑Fi associations, and standardize adapter placement and power to gather consistent data.

content.html:
Definition
Hardware essentials
External Wi‑Fi adapters
Offer better sensitivity, consistency, and sometimes support for wide channel scanning across 2.4 and 5 GHz.
Laptop configuration
Disable internal card associations and ensure survey software is linked to external adapters only.
Power and ergonomics
Charge batteries or use a power bank and secure cables to avoid trips during the walk.
Software and checks

Use survey software that records continuous RF samples and produces heatmaps for RSSI and SNR. Verify adapters appear in the device list and that the software’s channel view updates in real time.

Quick check: disable internal Wi‑Fi, start software, confirm external adapter is selected.
Practical tip: standardize how you carry the laptop and adapter so orientation is consistent between surveys.
Key Takeaway

Reliable hardware and consistent configuration eliminate many sources of survey error.

screens.title: RSSI: what it measures and its limits
screens.subtitle: Signal power is useful — but incomplete without context

narration.text: RSSI measures the raw received signal power from detected access points. It is commonly used to generate heatmaps that show coverage strength and where signals fall below thresholds set for different applications. For example, a target RSSI of about -67 dBm is often used for voice coverage, and -70 dBm may be used for general data. However, RSSI alone cannot tell you whether the signal will deliver acceptable throughput or low latency because it does not include the background noise level. A frequent misconception is to treat a numeric RSSI value as a guarantee of performance. In reality, RSSI must be combined with the noise floor to calculate SNR. Also, RSSI from neighboring networks on the same channel will appear in heatmaps and can confuse interpretation if you do not identify which AP the reading came from. Use RSSI maps to find coverage gaps, then cross‑reference with SNR and channel utilization to decide on AP relocation, antenna changes, or power adjustments. RSSI is a first filter — essential, but not sufficient. RSSI: what it measures and its limits means rssi shows received signal power and highlights coverage gaps, but must be paired with noise and utilization data to predict real performance.. In practical terms, signal power is useful — but incomplete without context. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: RSSI caution
keyIdea.text: RSSI shows received signal power and highlights coverage gaps, but must be paired with noise and utilization data to predict real performance.

content.html:
Definition
RSSI: received signal strength

RSSI reports the power of a received Wi‑Fi signal in dBm. It produces heatmaps useful for spotting coverage gaps and validating that target levels for voice or data are met.

Use: detect coverage holes and verify target RSSI thresholds.
Limit: does not include background noise or channel activity.
Cross‑check: always pair with SNR and utilization data.
Quick calculation & example
# Example: interpreting RSSI
# Target for voice: -67 dBm
Measured RSSI at desk: -68 dBm
Action: consider moving AP or increasing power slightly
Key Takeaway

RSSI locates signal strength but not quality. Use it to find gaps, then analyze SNR and utilization.

screens.title: SNR: why signal relative to noise matters
screens.subtitle: Calculate SNR and use thresholds to assess usability

narration.text: SNR — Signal‑to‑Noise Ratio — is the difference between the desired signal (RSSI) and the ambient noise floor. It is a primary indicator of link quality because it measures how clearly a receiver can distinguish desired transmissions from background RF energy. Compute SNR by subtracting the noise floor from RSSI. For instance, an RSSI of -60 dBm with a noise floor of -90 dBm yields an excellent SNR of 30 dB, while the same RSSI with a noise floor of -70 dBm gives only 10 dB, which will cause retransmissions and poor throughput. Typical practical thresholds are at least 20–25 dB for general data and 25–30 dB or more for latency‑sensitive applications like voice. A common misconception is treating RSSI as sufficient; SNR exposes cases where a strong signal is overwhelmed by a noisy environment. Use SNR heatmaps to prioritize remediation: raise SNR by lowering noise sources, moving APs closer, or reducing transmit power of overlapping APs if they cause contention. Always state the SNR calculation when you present findings so stakeholders understand the quality assessment. SNR: why signal relative to noise matters means snr = rssi − noise floor. snr directly predicts quality; aim for 20–25 db for data and 25–30 db for voice-sensitive use.. In practical terms, calculate snr and use thresholds to assess usability. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: SNR formula
keyIdea.text: SNR = RSSI − Noise Floor. SNR directly predicts quality; aim for 20–25 dB for data and 25–30 dB for voice-sensitive use.

content.html:
Core Metric
SNR: signal relative to noise

SNR shows how much stronger the desired signal is than the background noise. Calculate it by subtracting the noise floor from RSSI and use SNR thresholds to decide if an area is suitable for voice or high‑bandwidth applications.

Rule of thumb: 20–25 dB for general data; 25–30 dB for voice.
Misconception: strong RSSI can still yield poor SNR if noise is high.
Calculation example
# SNR calculation
RSSI = -60 dBm
Noise floor = -90 dBm
SNR = RSSI - Noise floor = -60 - (-90) = 30 dB
Interpretation: excellent for voice and high throughput
Key Takeaway

Always include SNR in your findings. It explains whether RSSI will translate into usable throughput.

screens.title: Noise floor and channel utilization
screens.subtitle: Ambient RF energy and how busy channels affect capacity

narration.text: The noise floor is the ambient background RF energy present in the environment. A high noise floor reduces SNR and makes it harder for receivers to decode signals. Noise sources can be other Wi‑Fi networks, non‑Wi‑Fi devices, or environmental factors. Channel utilization measures how busy a channel is — the percentage of time it is used for transmissions. Even with good RSSI and SNR, high channel utilization can create bottlenecks because devices must wait for airtime, causing latency and throughput degradation. During a passive survey you will see channel utilization charts that indicate when channels exceed comfortable thresholds, often around 50–60% sustained use. Use channel utilization to identify congested channels and to decide whether reassigning channels or adding additional capacity is required. When presenting findings, show both noise floor maps and utilization graphs because they explain different failure modes: one affects signal quality, the other affects airtime and capacity. Noise floor and channel utilization means noise floor affects signal clarity and snr; channel utilization shows airtime congestion. both must be considered for reliable performance.. In practical terms, ambient rf energy and how busy channels affect capacity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Noise & utilization
keyIdea.text: Noise floor affects signal clarity and SNR; channel utilization shows airtime congestion. Both must be considered for reliable performance.

content.html:
Core Metric
Noise floor

Noise floor is ambient RF energy. A higher noise floor reduces SNR and hurts performance even if RSSI is moderate. Identify noisy areas to reduce interference sources or adjust AP placement.

Cause: other networks, non‑Wi‑Fi devices, or environment
Action: identify sources and mitigate where possible.
Channel utilization

Utilization is the percentage of time a channel is occupied. High utilization — for example sustained levels above 50–60% — indicates congestion that reduces effective throughput even with strong signals.

Interpretation: high utilization → consider channel reassignment or additional APs for capacity
Key Takeaway

Noise affects quality, utilization affects airtime and capacity. Both explain different symptoms.

screens.title: Co‑channel vs adjacent‑channel interference
screens.subtitle: How overlapping signals differ and how a passive survey reveals them

narration.text: Interference appears in two common forms: co‑channel interference and adjacent‑channel interference. Co‑channel interference occurs when multiple APs operate on the same channel with overlapping coverage; devices contend for airtime, causing reduced throughput for everyone. A passive survey will show multiple APs on the same channel with strong RSSI in the same location. Adjacent‑channel interference happens when APs use partially overlapping channels, such as closely spaced channels in 2.4 GHz; this causes spectral overlap and degrades performance even though channels are technically different. While ACI is often less obvious than CCI, it still reduces throughput and increases retransmissions. Passive surveys visualize which channels are occupied and where signals overlap so you can decide whether to change channels or adjust power. A practical rule is to examine both the channel map and SNR/ RSSI at problem locations; CCI shows the same channel used by several strong APs, while ACI shows overlapping channels with energy spread across adjacent frequencies. Your remediation options differ: CCI often needs channel reassignment or better AP separation, while ACI may require choosing non‑overlapping channels or changing channel widths.

keyIdea.title: Interference types
keyIdea.text: CCI is same‑channel contention for airtime; ACI is spectral overlap between adjacent channels. Passive surveys show both by channel maps and signal strength overlays.

content.html:
Comparison
Co‑channel interference (CCI)

CCI appears when multiple APs use the same channel and their coverage overlaps. The result is airtime contention and reduced throughput. A passive survey shows multiple APs on one channel with strong RSSI in the same area.

Remedy: channel reassignment, reduce transmit power, or physical separation.
Adjacent‑channel interference (ACI)

ACI occurs when APs operate on overlapping channels. It causes spectral bleed and degrades performance even when channels differ slightly. Passive surveys show overlapping channel energy rather than identical channel listings.

Remedy: choose non‑overlapping channels, reduce channel width, or reposition APs.
Key Takeaway

Both CCI and ACI reduce performance but require different diagnostics and fixes; passive surveys make them visible.

screens.title: Detecting rogue access points
screens.subtitle: Identify unauthorized SSIDs and understand their implications

narration.text: A passive survey can reveal rogue access points broadcasting SSIDs within your premises. A rogue AP may be an employee’s misplaced device, a misconfigured corporate AP, or a malicious device set up to lure users. The passive survey picks up any broadcast SSIDs and their signal strengths, and survey software often lets you place suspected rogues on the floor plan. The presence of an unauthorized SSID inside a secure area, such as a server room, is a red flag because it may bypass network controls and offer attackers a backdoor. When you detect a potential rogue, record its SSID, BSSID, channel, and approximate location. Then coordinate with security to physically locate and remove or reconfigure the device. Avoid assuming a nearby neighbor is the cause: if the SSID is located on your floor plan inside your walls, treat it as an on‑premises device. The passive survey is therefore a critical security tool as well as a performance tool. Detecting rogue access points means passive surveys list broadcasting ssids and their locations so you can identify and remediate unauthorized access points that risk network security.. In practical terms, identify unauthorized ssids and understand their implications. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Rogue detection
keyIdea.text: Passive surveys list broadcasting SSIDs and their locations so you can identify and remediate unauthorized access points that risk network security.

content.html:
Security
Detecting rogue APs

Passive surveys reveal all broadcasting SSIDs and their signal strengths. If an unauthorized SSID appears inside your mapped floor plan, treat it as a rogue device requiring investigation and remediation.

Record: SSID, BSSID, channel, approximate location on the floor plan.
Security risk: unauthorized APs can bypass network controls and provide access to internal resources.
Scenario

If you find an SSID like "FREE_WIFI_GUEST" broadcasting from inside a server room, this strongly suggests a rogue AP and requires immediate action.

Action steps: document details, notify security, locate and remove or reconfigure the device.
Key Takeaway

Treat on‑premises unauthorized SSIDs as high‑priority security issues and coordinate removal immediately.

screens.title: Interpreting passive survey data points
screens.subtitle: Practice calculating SNR and diagnosing three sample locations

narration.text: Now practice interpreting real passive survey data by calculating SNR and assessing potential issues at three locations. For each data point compute SNR by subtracting the noise floor from RSSI. Use that SNR plus channel utilization and neighbor AP readings to identify coverage gaps, capacity problems, or interference. For Location A, a strong RSSI combined with a very low noise floor typically indicates good conditions for both voice and data. For Location B, moderate RSSI but a high noise floor or high channel utilization will point to capacity or interference issues rather than simple coverage problems. For Location C, low RSSI combined with nearby neighbor APs on the same channel suggests a coverage gap that may be worsened by co‑channel contention. When you present your conclusions, include the numeric SNR, identify which metric is the limiting factor, and recommend a concrete action such as moving an AP, changing channels, or investigating a rogue device. This practice turns survey numbers into actionable decisions. Interpreting passive survey data points means calculate snr for each data point and combine with channel utilization and neighbor ap info to determine coverage, capacity, or interference issues and propose actions.. In practical terms, practice calculating snr and diagnosing three sample locations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Interpretation practice
keyIdea.text: Calculate SNR for each data point and combine with channel utilization and neighbor AP info to determine coverage, capacity, or interference issues and propose actions.

content.html:
Hands‑on Activity
Data point interpretation

Calculate SNR for each location and then reason about coverage, interference, and capacity. Present a one‑line recommendation for each point.

# Location A: Open Office
RSSI = -55 dBm
Noise floor = -92 dBm
SNR = -55 - (-92) = 37 dB
Interpretation: strong SNR, low noise, low utilization → good coverage and capacity

# Location B: Conference Room
RSSI = -68 dBm
Noise floor = -75 dBm
SNR = -68 - (-75) = 7 dB
Interpretation: low SNR, high channel utilization → capacity and interference problems

# Location C: Corner Office
RSSI = -82 dBm
Noise floor = -90 dBm
SNR = -82 - (-90) = 8 dB
Interpretation: poor RSSI and low SNR; likely coverage gap and neighbor AP influence
Example conclusions & actions
Action for A

No change required; verify across a second walk and monitor utilization if density increases.

Action for B

Investigate neighbor AP on same channel and high utilization; consider channel change or additional capacity for meetings.

Action for C

Address coverage gap by moving AP closer or adding an AP; check client orientation and obstacles.

screens.title: Common mistakes, safety, and next steps
screens.subtitle: Avoid rushed walks, bad sampling, and equipment risks

narration.text: Several common mistakes reduce the value of a passive survey. Rushing the walk or failing to take enough data points produces incomplete heatmaps. Inconsistent orientation or adapter placement introduces variability between runs, and relying only on internal laptop Wi‑Fi instead of an external adapter can make your results inconsistent or less sensitive. Another common error is interpreting RSSI in isolation; without SNR and noise floor, you can miss the underlying cause of poor performance. From a safety perspective ensure your laptop is charged, cables are secured, and you remain aware of surroundings while walking and looking at the screen. Secure equipment to prevent accidental drops or theft. screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Three essential ideas from passive surveys

narration.text: Remember three core ideas: first, a passive site survey passively listens to the air to produce ground truth about coverage, noise, and interference; it does not associate to access points. Second, RSSI is useful for mapping signal power but must be combined with noise floor and SNR to judge usable performance; channel utilization adds airtime context for capacity. Third, passive surveys are security tools as well as performance tools — they reveal rogue access points and show where immediate remediation is needed. Use these three ideas as a checklist when you plan, execute, and analyze a passive survey so your findings lead to targeted, evidence‑based changes in AP placement, power, and channel choices. screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders for fieldwork and analysis

narration.text: Keep three practical reminders in mind while conducting passive surveys. First, standardize your kit and technique — external adapters, disabled internal association, consistent orientation and pace — so data is repeatable. Second, always interpret RSSI in context: calculate SNR with the noise floor and check channel utilization to distinguish coverage problems from capacity or interference issues. Third, treat SSID lists from your survey as a security inventory: any unauthorized SSID mapped inside your space must be investigated and remediated. These reminders will help you collect reliable data, draw correct conclusions, and produce recommendations that reduce user complaints and security risk.
